Epinephrine is a chemical your body naturally makes and releases into your blood during moments of stress, danger, or excitement. It rapidly prepares your entire body to either fight a threat or run away from it.
The Name Itself

The word epinephrine comes from Greek and Latin roots:

  • "Epi" means above or upon
  • "Nephros" means kidney

Put together, it literally means "above the kidney" — which is a direct reference to where it's produced in your body (more on that in a moment).

You've almost certainly heard its other name: adrenaline. These two words refer to the exact same molecule. The difference is purely historical and regional — "adrenaline" is preferred in the UK and in everyday speech, while "epinephrine" is the official scientific and medical term used in the United States and in pharmacology worldwide. When doctors give you an injection of it, they call it epinephrine. When someone says your "adrenaline is pumping," they mean the same thing.
What Kind of Molecule Is It?

Epinephrine belongs to a class of molecules called catecholamines — a family of chemical messengers that are made from the amino acid tyrosine (which you get from protein-rich foods like meat, eggs, and cheese).

More specifically, epinephrine is both a hormone and a neurotransmitter:

  • As a hormone, it's released into the bloodstream and travels throughout the entire body to affect multiple organs at once.
  • As a neurotransmitter, it transmits signals between nerve cells in certain parts of the nervous system.

Think of it like a broadcast emergency alert — when it's released, it doesn't just send a message to one place. It goes everywhere at once.
Where Is It Made?

Epinephrine is produced in your adrenal glands — two small, triangular-shaped glands that sit right on top of each of your kidneys (hence the name "above the kidney"). Each gland has two distinct regions. The outer region is called the adrenal cortex, and the inner region is called the adrenal medulla. Epinephrine is made in the adrenal medulla.

The adrenal medulla is essentially a specialized part of your nervous system. The cells there (called chromaffin cells) act like modified nerve cells that, instead of sending an electrical signal to the next nerve, dump their chemical messenger — epinephrine — directly into the bloodstream.

A small amount of epinephrine is also produced and used directly within the brain as a neurotransmitter, but the bulk of what affects your body during stress comes from the adrenal glands.
How Is It Released?

Your body doesn't just randomly release epinephrine. There's a precise chain of command:

  1. Your brain detects something stressful or dangerous — real or perceived. This could be a car swerving toward you, public speaking, or even an exciting movie.
  2. The brain's hypothalamus (the command center for survival responses) sends a signal.
  3. This signal travels through your sympathetic nervous system — the branch of your nervous system responsible for activating the body in stressful situations.
  4. A nerve fiber directly connects to the adrenal medulla and triggers it to release epinephrine into the blood.
  5. Because this is a direct nerve-to-gland connection, the response is lightning fast — epinephrine hits your bloodstream within seconds.

This is different from many other hormones that go through slower chains of chemical signals. Epinephrine's pathway is built for speed.
What Does It Actually Do to Your Body?

Epinephrine works by binding to specific receptors (think of these as locks, and epinephrine is the key) found on the surface of cells in many different organs. When it binds to these receptors, it triggers specific changes in that organ. These receptors are called adrenergic receptors, and there are different types (alpha and beta), which is why epinephrine has such wide-ranging effects.

Here's what happens throughout the body:

Heart

  • Your heart beats faster and more forcefully. This pumps more blood to where it's needed most — your muscles and brain.

Lungs

  • The airways in your lungs (bronchioles) widen (dilate), allowing more oxygen to flow in with each breath. This is why your breathing quickens during stress.

Blood Vessels

  • Blood vessels near your skin and digestive organs contract (narrow), reducing blood flow to those areas.
  • Blood vessels in your muscles dilate (widen), delivering more oxygenated blood to your limbs so you can run or fight.
  • Your blood pressure rises as a result of all this.

Liver

  • Your liver rapidly breaks down stored glycogen into glucose (blood sugar) and releases it into the blood. Your muscles and brain need fuel, and epinephrine ensures an instant energy supply.

Fat Cells

  • Fat is also broken down and released into the blood as free fatty acids — additional fuel for your muscles.

Eyes

  • Your pupils dilate (widen), letting in more light so you can see your environment more clearly.

Skin

  • You may notice goosebumps, pale skin, or sweating — classic signs of epinephrine activity.

Digestion

  • Non-essential functions like digestion are temporarily slowed down or shut off. Your body's priority is survival, not processing your lunch.

Pain Perception

  • Epinephrine can temporarily reduce pain sensitivity. This is why people sometimes don't feel injuries until the danger has passed.
The Fight-or-Flight Response

All of those effects above happen together, almost simultaneously, and they collectively form what is called the fight-or-flight response — a term coined by the physiologist Walter Cannon in the early 20th century.

The idea is elegantly simple: in the wild, when a predator approaches, an animal (or ancient human) has two survival choices — stand and fight, or run away. Epinephrine prepares the body optimally for both options by:

  • Maximizing oxygen and fuel delivery to muscles
  • Sharpening the senses
  • Suppressing everything that isn't immediately necessary for survival

This response evolved over millions of years and is found across virtually all vertebrate animals. It's one of the most ancient and conserved survival mechanisms in biology. The challenge in modern humans is that the same system is triggered by non-life-threatening stressors — a work deadline, an argument, or anxiety — when there's no predator to fight or flee from. Chronic activation of this system is one reason long-term stress is harmful to health.
How the Body Turns It Off

The body is careful not to stay in fight-or-flight mode indefinitely. Once the stressor passes:

  • Epinephrine is rapidly broken down in the blood by enzymes called COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) and MAO (monoamine oxidase). Its half-life in the blood is only about 1–3 minutes — meaning it's gone very quickly.
  • The broken-down products are excreted in urine.
  • The parasympathetic nervous system (the "rest and digest" counterpart to the sympathetic system) becomes dominant again, calming everything back down.

This is why after a frightening experience, you might feel a sudden wave of relaxation or even exhaustion — your body is returning to its baseline, and the fuel that was burned needs to be replenished.
Medical Uses of Epinephrine

Because epinephrine is such a powerful activator of the body, it has critical medical applications:

Anaphylaxis (Severe Allergic Reactions)

This is the most well-known medical use. During a life-threatening allergic reaction, the body releases chemicals that cause blood vessels to dilate wildly and airways to constrict — a potentially fatal combination. Epinephrine rapidly reverses all of this: it constricts blood vessels, raises blood pressure, and opens the airways. The EpiPen is a pre-loaded device that injects epinephrine automatically — it can be the difference between life and death.

Cardiac Arrest

When the heart stops beating, epinephrine is injected to stimulate it. It's a standard drug in resuscitation protocols (CPR + defibrillation + epinephrine is the classic combination).

Asthma and Severe Breathing Problems

By opening the airways, epinephrine can relieve life-threatening bronchospasm (sudden tightening of the airways).

Local Anesthesia

Dentists often mix epinephrine with local anesthetics (like lidocaine). The epinephrine constricts blood vessels at the injection site, which keeps the anesthetic from washing away too quickly — making the numbing effect last longer and reducing bleeding.

Septic Shock

In patients with dangerously low blood pressure due to severe infection (septic shock), epinephrine is used to constrict blood vessels and raise blood pressure back to survivable levels.
What Happens When There's Too Much or Too Little?

Too Much (Excess Epinephrine)

A tumor called a pheochromocytoma can form in the adrenal medulla and secrete excessive epinephrine (and a related hormone, norepinephrine) in unpredictable bursts. Symptoms include sudden episodes of rapid heartbeat, severe headache, sweating, and dangerously high blood pressure. It's rare but serious.

Chronically high stress also keeps epinephrine levels elevated longer than is healthy, contributing to hypertension (high blood pressure), heart disease, anxiety disorders, and immune suppression over time.

Too Little (Insufficient Epinephrine)

Because epinephrine is one of multiple overlapping systems the body uses to respond to stress, isolated epinephrine deficiency is rare. However, people who have had their adrenal glands removed or damaged may struggle to mount a normal stress response and can experience a condition called adrenal insufficiency, where the body cannot respond adequately to physical stressors like illness or injury.
Epinephrine vs. Norepinephrine — What's the Difference?

Epinephrine has a close chemical cousin called norepinephrine (also called noradrenaline). They are structurally very similar — norepinephrine is actually the direct chemical precursor to epinephrine (your body makes norepinephrine first, then converts it to epinephrine by adding a small chemical group).

Their effects overlap but differ in emphasis:

  • Norepinephrine primarily constricts blood vessels and raises blood pressure. It's the dominant neurotransmitter of the sympathetic nervous system at most nerve-to-organ junctions.
  • Epinephrine does all of the above plus has stronger effects on the heart, metabolism (breaking down glucose and fats), and airway dilation.

Together, they orchestrate the full fight-or-flight response.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

ConceptThe Takeaway

Epinephrine is your body's emergency chemical alarm. Made in the adrenal glands sitting above your kidneys, it's released in seconds when your brain senses danger. It floods your bloodstream and simultaneously commands your heart to pump harder, your lungs to open wider, your muscles to receive more fuel, and everything non-essential to pause — all in service of one goal: keeping you alive in a crisis. It's also a life-saving drug used in medicine for allergic reactions, cardiac arrest, and more. In minutes, it breaks down and the body returns to calm. It is one of the most elegant, fast, and powerful molecules in all of biology.
